title: Chapter 11 — The Interview
text:
Sable's relay came in on a Thursday, which was how he knew the job was real — she never routed him hypotheticals.

Her voice laid it out the way she laid out everything she couldn't fully vet: once, clearly, without the easy language she used when she'd checked every angle and liked what she saw. The contract summary scrolled up on his display as she talked, a plain-text overlay with none of the polish she usually dressed a clean offer in.

"<entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus Syndicate</entity>, <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> cell," she said. "<entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>'s arm. They want a quarterly arrangement — discretionary security consults, off-book, paid at market plus twenty percent. The twenty is for the discretion." A cursor blinked at the bottom of the fee line, waiting on nothing. "The catch: they want an audition first. Their word. Three operatives, controlled corridor, no kill brief. They want to watch you fight before they buy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the line. The fee was exactly what she'd said — market plus twenty, quarterly, no retainer. A clean offer.

"What's the problem?" he asked.

"The problem," Sable said, "is that the <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> is the one client in this city I can't vet. Not because I haven't tried. Their security is better than my tools, and they know it, and they know that I know it, and the offer still puts no vetting on the page." Her voice didn't move to close the file. "My rule is my rule for a reason."

He knew the reason. If she couldn't vet the client, she couldn't pull him out if it went wrong. A fixer who couldn't pull her freelancer out wasn't a fixer anymore.

She wasn't hiding any of it. That was the point of the plain text. She was laying it out so he could see the seam — exactly where the liability lived and who it landed on if something tore — and handing him the choice with the map already drawn.

"Your call," she said. She meant it. The file sat open on his display, waiting for a decision.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the twenty percent on a quarterly contract. He thought about who <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> was, and what the <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> built its parallel city out of, and which parts of that he could work beside and which he couldn't. And he thought about the code — cut everything, cross nothing. It had never told him who deserved to be cut. It only told him where his own line was.

He reached to close the file himself. On the line, a half-second of <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9c-7d8b-85dd-a3103991418b">dead air</entity> — not a dropped connection, just Sable choosing not to fill the silence before he decided. She was good at silence. She let it work. Then the line picked back up.

"Then it's on me," he said. "Not on you. I take this, the Gennaro rule stays clean — you didn't vet a client I chose without you."

Sable was quiet for a beat. "That's a careful distinction."

"It's the one that keeps your rule working."

She let that sit for one more second. Then, already moving on, not warming the line to say goodbye properly: "The audition is Tuesday. The address is on the back."

He told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> where he was going — the logistics, the timeline, the gear state — and she took it in the way she took in all his logistics: listening through the information for the actual sentence.

"<entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>," she said when he was done. Under the bench a small speaker was playing a baseball game from a season that had ended before either of them was born, the announcer low and unhurried, the crowd a steady tide she wasn't listening to so much as keeping company with. She was reseating a lens element on the bench, both eyes on the optic. A prosthetic eye, the cheap mass-market kind, in for a rebuild she wasn't charging for. A courier two blocks over had taken a curb too fast and cracked the iris diaphragm, and the maker wanted more for the part than the woman earned in a month. On the far end of the bench, outside the work zone, sat a small analog barometer she'd once told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was broken. It hadn't moved in three years. She kept it anyway. She said she liked the shape of certain kinds of useless. "<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> arm."

"Quarterly arrangement."

"Mm." She turned the element in the light, checking the seat. "I can't monitor your array at the other end. Whatever they run in those corridors, I'm blind on your diagnostics until you come home."

"I know."

She set the element down and looked at her hands, which she did when she was deciding something. "Your forearm held the last one. It'll hold this one." She went back to the optic. "Come back in a number of pieces I can count."

He reached for the diagnostic cuff on the bench — the one thing he'd meant to leave with a fresh baseline, so at least the array would log its own faults for her to read after — and the cuff woke gray. No handshake. He tried the reseat twice, thumbing the contact band flat against the mesh the way she'd taught him, waiting for the display to bloom into the lattice map it should have thrown in half a second. Nothing bloomed. The third time it threw a checksum error and went dark for good, and they both knew there wasn't another in the drawer and no time to source one before the quarterly window closed. She'd built that cuff from salvage and spite, and the read-side of it cost what the courier's eye cost, more than most people made in a month, and neither salvage nor spite would rebuild it before Tuesday. Not just blind at the far end now. Blind from the moment he walked out the door, the array running unwitnessed through corridors neither of them could name, with no record of its own failing to bring home.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't look up. But her hands had stopped.

He weighed it — walk it back, lose the window, keep the safety net; or take the arm out into the dark with no one watching it, not even itself. He set the dead cuff down on the far end of the bench, next to the barometer that hadn't moved in three years.

He packed the gear. He left the door open the width she kept it.

The <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> basement was a cleared corridor, fifty feet, load-bearing columns down its length — the kind of space that had spent years as a live-fire range and kept the habit in the concrete. <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> stood at the far end under a lamp, hands folded, gray qipao. She did not greet him. The contract hadn't started yet.

Mira was at the near end.

She was not compact and she was not warm. She was the kind of tall you only notice when she turns to show the profile — the length of a person used to being the last thing in a room that still moves. She read <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> the way a captain reads a unit report: all the way through, back to front, spending a beat on the sutured seam in his forearm and the stance that gave away the hip tape even though the tape wasn't showing.

"The brief," she said. Her voice had already settled the friendliness question and moved on to the one she cared about. "Three operatives. Live hardware, safety profile on. The test isn't whether you can clear the corridor."

"What's the test?" he asked.

"I'll tell you at the end." She stepped aside.

The first came from behind the left column at the eight-foot mark — better positioning than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> usually saw at this level. Ceramic wrist plates, a shock-baton, and the spare stride of a woman who fought the way she did everything else: as little as it took to reach the outcome. She led with a combination that read textbook, efficient angles, no wasted motion. He caught her baton arm on the third swing with the column at his back and put her down with her own momentum. The baton rang off concrete. She stayed down and said count — the range word for stopped.

The second came from both sides at once. A pair, not one, which the brief hadn't mentioned. One was a feint. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array priced it in half a second. He took the real one first on the inside line, shoulder to the column, and the feinter ran into the fact that his partner was already sitting down. Two counts.

The third was at the twenty-foot mark, already moving before the second was finished, and she was the corridor kind of good — the kind you only get by being ambushed in one and living through it. She came with a blade on the left and a thumb ring on the right, and the thumb ring was the one to solve.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> shoulder come in.

He didn't have to. The array had the clean version — the forward pivot, the outside line, the disarm — all of it at 6.2% risk on his current hardware. He could have taken her clean and paid nothing.

He let it come in because the taser was the point. The taser would fire no matter what he did to <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> arm. So the array gave him the other read: take the shoulder to get inside the taser's radius before it cycled. The shoulder would cost. The floor was concrete.

The taser fired into his upper back and the charge rode his mesh. His left hand closed on nothing. His jaw locked. Every nerve down his left side, shoulder to hip, lit up with the kind of thing that usually ends the sentence — his vision pixelating for a half-second, the array throwing micro-stutters as the implant rerouted around the electrical load — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drove both boots into her center while the charge was still running. She hit the column and sat down hard and said count.

He stood in the corridor a moment while the left side of his body caught up to the damage. The array was already running diagnostics on the burn, pricing the reroute against the firmware that would have to hold it — the kind of bill that came due later, in a shop, in cash, not now.

Three counts. Five seconds.

At the far end, <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>'s hands stayed folded.

Mira walked the corridor toward him — not toward, exactly. More like a captain inspecting an experiment she'd already formed a guess about.

"You had the outside line on the third one," she said.

"I had it."

"Forward pivot, full disarm, taser out of reach. Six-point-two percent on your hardware state."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her. "You ran the array geometry?"

"We ran your file." She looked at where the taser had caught him — the burn already darkening the mesh weave where the charge had grounded through. At the sutured forearm. Back up. "You chose the expensive version."

"Inside radius before it cycled. Cheaper than six percent on a pivot I might not finish."

"No," she said. "You could have finished it. I watched you price the clean version for a third of a second before you moved. The one where the shoulder never gets touched. You took the one where you absorb it instead." She studied him. "She's got a three-day-old mesh repair on her left knee. Stairs, not a fight. Your array had the read."

"I had the read," he said.

"The code," Mira said. "<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> everything, cross nothing. The cross-nothing part." She wasn't asking.

"That's the code."

She looked at his back where the taser had fired, the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> looked at a diagnostic she already knew the answer to. "Cost you a rib."

"Probably two."

"You want <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> medical."

"I want <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>."

She made no comment on it. It was a preference she understood. "The arrangement," she said. "<entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> will want it quarterly. I want first call on the discretionary consults. Standard rate plus the twenty for both." She looked at him with the flat attention of someone who had stopped measuring him and started setting terms. "I don't need your fixer's vetting channel. I'll handle my own."

"She'll notice that."

"She will." No apology in it, just the fact. "What I need from a <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>-adjacent freelancer is someone the <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> doesn't own. Your fixer keeps you that way. I'm not asking you to cut the channel — I'm asking you to keep it separate from mine." A pause. "Those are different asks."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned them over. The left side of his body was still lit up with the ghost of the charge, the deep kind that told him the shoulder would be reminding him for three days.

"Friday," he said. "Standard rate. We start there."

Mira nodded once, the way she probably nodded at everything that landed where she expected. "There's a man in the Narrows I want you to see before you leave. A togishi. He'll want to look at <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>." She looked at <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> at his hip — not with the combat read she'd given it in the corridor, but with something quieter. "Let him."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-e248-74dd-b603-8b19f4c3ad6a">The togishi of the Narrows</entity> worked out of a two-room shop three blocks from the cherry trees, down a flight of stairs polished smooth by forty years of foot traffic and the weight of blades going in and coming out. The sign on the door was a single character, brushed by hand. It said nothing useful to anyone who hadn't already been sent.

He received <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across both palms, blunt spine toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the way a bow receives a blade — not surrender, courtesy. An acknowledgment between people who understand that the steel is the point.

He did not speak for three minutes. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the outer room and waited, the ribs keeping up their steady complaint. The togishi held <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> to the single overhead lamp and turned it, slow, and the steel caught the light and threw it back fractured — not the clean reflection of folded metal, but something that bent light the way water does.

The togishi returned <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> the way he had taken it and stood at the worktable with his hands at his sides.

"How long have you carried it?"

"Eleven years."

"Before that."

"I don't remember."

The togishi looked at him. Not at <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. "You don't remember."

"I was given it. I don't remember the giving."

The old man turned back to the worktable. "The work is skilled. Not excellent — skilled." He laid two fingers flat on <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>, near the hamon, the way a doctor reads a pulse. "I cannot tell you what it's made of. This is none of the alloys I know, and not a blend of any of them. Not folded. Not hammered the way steel is hammered. Whatever is in this edge, I don't know the door you'd walk through to buy it." He ran his thumb down the spine, never the edge — the safe way, a gesture forty years had made look like nothing. "There's no school in it either. The finishing cuts are the maker's own — the hand made a decision at the end that isn't in any lineage I know."

"Is that a problem?"

"It is an observation." He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. "I have held perhaps eight thousand blades in my life. Every one of them has a history I can read some part of. This one remembers nothing I can read. The steel is good. The work is honest. The edge is precise." He set his palm flat on the saya. "It is the loneliest piece of steel I have held."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s thumb had moved to the top of the tsuka, up against the guard, without him deciding to move it.

"There is one thing more." The togishi's hand did not leave the saya. "A blade that reads as nothing was made to read as nothing. Eight thousand blades and I have never seen a hand work this hard to leave no name." He turned <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> once more, and where a maker's mark should have sat on the tang there was only clean metal — no scratch, no hesitation, no place where a tool had slipped or a hand had wavered. "Someone did not merely forge this. Someone erased it — and did it well enough that I, who have spent my life learning to read steel, cannot find the seam. To erase a blade this completely you must know exactly what you are undoing. You must know the maker's hand well enough to unmake it without leaving a trace of the unmaking." He drew his palm back slowly, as though the metal had grown warm. "Which means whoever put it in your hands did not want you to know where it came from. And whoever wants that has reasons you have not begun to weigh." His eyes moved from <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face and stayed there. "You came to me hoping to learn one small thing. Instead you have learned that the small thing was buried on purpose, by someone with the skill to bury it and the will to keep it buried. That is not an answer. That is a door with no handle on your side."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing.

"You came because someone sent you," the togishi said. "Not because you wanted the answer."

"That's right."

"Come back when you want the answer." He bowed. "The blade is well. I have no repair for you."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> bowed. He left the answer in the room.

Mira was waiting on the block above the stairs, leaning against the cherry-blossom gate — not impatient, not comfortable, just letting the minutes go.

"Well?" she asked.

"Skilled, not excellent. No lineage."

She made no comment on what else the togishi had said. She'd sent him. She already knew what he'd say.

"A thing came to my desk last week," she said, in the tone she used for things she'd decided were his to know. "The desk that bought your file from <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> — the one through <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> Civic. The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> requisition."

"I know about that one." He wanted it to land as fact, something he already owned, so she'd give him the next thing and not the lecture. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s dead-ended. <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>'s a shell. There's nothing there to chase, so tell me who's actually moving."

"That's exactly the wrong thing to have decided," she said, and the mildness of it was the worst part. "You just told me you've stopped looking at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. Which means whoever bought you through <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> now knows the one door you'll never check twice is the one they came through. You didn't close that file, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. You marked it *safe* — out loud, to me, on a public block. That's not intelligence you own. That's a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa7f-70d6-91c0-e2616dbd90a6">blind spot</entity> you just advertised."

She let him sit in that a moment.

"Then you know there's more than one buyer now. Plural subscribers in the last four weeks, neither through <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. One is architecture I don't recognize — patient, months old, routes clean. It's not pulling your file. It's watching who pulls your file." She tilted her head, as if the distinction cost her something. "The other is four weeks old and loud enough that I caught it from here." She looked at the cherry trees, past their bloom now and just trees again. "Somebody with more patience than budget found you at the same time as somebody with more budget than patience. They're not working together. Which means two different people decided you were worth watching in the same month." A pause. "Ask the Antiquarian who else subscribes."

"He won't sell me my own file."

"Ask him anyway. There may be a thing he'll tell you that he hasn't decided to sell." She buttoned the third button on her coat, which was her tell for a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa8f-796a-8b70-7076ec482c7f">clean exit</entity>, and stepped off the gate. "Friday. Standard rate. We'll start there."

"Friday," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

She was three steps down the stairs when she stopped, and the stopping was worse than anything she'd said standing still. "The four-week one," she said, not turning around. "I told you I caught it from here. I didn't tell you how. It pinged my desk this morning — my desk, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, which means it's stopped watching you and started watching the people who watch you. That's not a subscriber anymore. That's someone drawing a map of everyone you'd run to." She let that sit. "So Friday isn't where we start. Friday is where I find out how much of my own network I just lit up by sending a togishi to look at your face. I don't know yet which of us the loud one is really following. Neither do you. And I don't have a Friday-shaped answer for that."

She left the way she'd found him — without ceremony, without looking back, the way she treated everything she'd already decided.

He rode home through the Narrows. The taser burn, the togishi's word, two new names on his file — none of it would sit still at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> volume.

<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">The Narrows</entity> was the strip of low blocks where the freight viaduct cut the district in half and rents dropped to whatever the noise didn't drive off. At this hour a woman was hosing fish blood off a loading dock into a drain that had stopped draining years ago. The blood spread across the concrete and pooled at the curb, and nobody looked twice, because nobody looked twice at anything here after midnight. That was the whole arrangement. He rode through with his lights low, and the Narrows let him pass the way it let everyone pass who didn't need it to be anything else. You paid the toll in attention — <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa7-7ac0-be88-cb8b1ce7644e">eyes up</entity>, hands visible, business your own — and the strip left you alone.

The burn reported up the left side on every seam in the pavement, shoulder to hip. A cost already paid. He breathed around it, a negotiation now, in and out, and kept the throttle even. The hurt had the same weight whether he moved slow or fast, so he kept it steady and let it have its momentum.

The togishi's word wouldn't leave him. Loneliest. Eight thousand blades through those hands, forty years of knowing what steel remembered, and that was the one he'd reached for — that, and the open door behind it. Come back when you want the answer. Which meant the answer was there. Which meant he wasn't looking for it yet. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the corner at Madison a fraction wider than the surface needed.

The city came back around him — the overnight freight, the gray-zone markets cracking their first windows, the particular thickness of a block that had been cooking its own air for thirty years. Above the industrial district the air shimmered where the processors did their work, pushing the weather where the corpos wanted it. Not here. Here got what the rest of the city didn't want. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter would be dark by now. Across the hall, a light would be on.

He thought about asking <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> to chase the harmonic again. She read systems the way the togishi read steel — she'd hear its whole history in the hum, tell him whether that clean tone underneath the noise was a bleed, a feedback loop, a piece of machinery running where it shouldn't. Not the answer — he wasn't built for the answer yet. Just what it was, without where it came from.

And there it snagged. Because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't answer half-questions. Ask her the harmonic and she'd want the source, and the source was the two new names on his file, and the names were the taser burn, and the burn was the togishi's open door — pull one thread and the whole knot came with it. She'd read the omissions faster than the query. She always did. He could picture it exactly: the door open before he knocked, her hands still on some piece of hardware she wouldn't set down, *you look like someone folded you in half*, and then the quiet while she did the math he was already doing. She wouldn't ask where he'd been. She wouldn't have to. The knowing would sit in the room between them like a third person. He could keep it from her and get nothing, or hand it over and lose the last piece of this that was only his. Every way he turned it, the ask cost more than the answer was worth tonight, and the not-asking cost him the sleep he wasn't going to get anyway.

He rode the last blocks home.

He was three blocks from <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> when the relay pinged.

Not a job.
